# Tree-based thinking

So far we have focused on learning how to construct _slendr_ demographic
models, how to compute basic summary statistics, and demonstrating how
exploratory, simulation-based workflows help us study the behavior and
limitations of statistics of interest.

In this chapter, we will change the pace a bit, and introduce the power of
_slendr_ as a bit of an "interactive popgen calculator" to quickly explore
theoretical concepts in a hands-on way, and build intuition into how (and why)
these concepts work the way they do. We will also dig a little bit more into
the tree-sequence data itself.

Our main focus here will be on $f$-statistics, mostly because they form such a
crucial component of population genomics research, specifically within the aDNA
context, and because they showcase very nicely why simulation-based exploration
can be so powerful. In the process, we will also learn a few useful _slendr_
tricks which are applicable for many other research problems.









## Exercise: "Outgroup" $f_3$ as a measure of overlap of tree paths

To ease into the problem of interpreting $f$-statistics as measures of
overlapping paths in "population trees" or---when admixture comes into the
picture---in "admixture graphs", let's briefly return to our familiar $f_3$
statistic.

**Create a new script `f_null.R` and paste the following code into that
script. As always, read through the code, try to build a mental model of what
it's going to do, then run it and compare your understanding with the generated
visualization of the model.**

(I know this is easy, but being able to read code quickly and efficiently is
the best way to learn to spot bugs.)

```{r}
#| output: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

# build a basic population tree structure
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

# compile the model and define recording of individuals
model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)
schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

# plot the model to check its correctness visually
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

# simulate 10 Mb of genomic data for later exploration
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

---

Now, consider the model implemented in our script `f_null.R`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)
```

We know from [the theory of
$f$-statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214)
that:

- $f_2(A, B)$ statistic measures the branch length between A and B (two
individuals, two groups of individuals, two populations, etc.), and

- similarly, $f_3(C; A, B)$ statistic is formally defined as the branch length
which connects the internal most recent common ancestor node of A and B with
the lineage C,

- the same also applies to $f_4$ which we will discuss later.

This can be seen graphically in [Figure
1](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/figure/379128872/1485fig1.jpeg) of that
linked paper.

Another thing established in the paper is the fact that any $f$-statistic can
be expressed as a linear combination of multiple $f_2$ statistics. If you're
not familiar with linear algebra, this might sound a bit obscure, but the idea
is simple. More concretely, for instance, equation (20b) in the same paper
states the following, which decomposes an $f_3$ statistic into a composite of
simpler $f_2$ statistics (this is what "linear combination" basically is):

$$f_3(A; B, C) = \frac{1}{2} (f_2(A, C) + f_2(A, B) - f_2(B, C))$$

---

**Draw a sketch of the population p1, p2, p3, etc. model plotted above on a
piece of paper, then trace by hand the paths indicated by the three $f_2$
statistics in this equation on that drawn model (again, knowing that $f_2(A,
B)$ describes the branch between some two nodes $A$ and $B$. When you "add" and
"subtract" paths based on the equation (graphically! on your drawn model), do
you arrive at the definition of "outgroup" $f_3$ as we defined it above?**


---

True story: When I was writing this chapter, I made a mistake in the equation
above, which I discovered after I wrote a quick simulation to double-check that
the equation is correct. Let's retrace my steps here because it shows why even
very quick simulations can be really useful (almost like a "popgen
calculator"!).

**Let's move to R. Use the function `ts_f2()` to implement this equation in
code, computing a "homemade" $f_3(A = p4; B = p1, C = p2)$ statistic which you
just solved on paper, and compare it to the result produced by `ts_f3()`
provided by _slendr_. Do you get the same result using both methods, thus
verifying that the equation is correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

First let's get our groups of individuals in the tree sequence so that we can
refer to grouped individuals more easily:

```{r}
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
s
```

Let's compose a "homemade" $f_3$ statistic as a linear combination of $f_2$
statistics as given by the equation:

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- 1/2 * (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"])$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"])$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"])$f2
)
homemade_f3
```

Finally, let's compute $f_3$ using the "official" built-in _slendr_ function:

```{r}
simulated_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"])
simulated_f3
```

You can see that the `ts_f3()` implementation gives basically the same value as
our "homemade" implementation based on a linear combination of $f_2$
statistics, just as predicted by the underlying math!

:::









## Exercise: Mutations versus branches

Do you recall how I told you that you don't have to add mutations to your tree
sequence `ts`, and still be able to compute population genetic statistics? But
that you can safely add them with `ts_mutate()` anyway?

The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a
mathematical [duality between mutation-based and branch-based
statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/215/3/779/5930459)---it
actually doesn't matter which way we compute our statistics, they give
mathematically the same result in terms of theoretical statistical expectations
(i.e., expectations of what happen in real data).

---

**Repeat the previous exercise, but this time specify `mode = "branch"` in all
your `ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()` commands.** I suggest that you make a copy of your
`ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()`-based code in your `f_null.R` script and and modify the
copies for easier comparison. **What numbers do you get compared to the results
of the previous exercise in terms of their scale? Can you relate those values
to what your population tree model visualization indicates (in terms of branch
lenghts)? Look at your sketch with pen and paper again if this helps in
understanding the branch length (particularly with regards to split times).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"], mode = "branch")
```

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], mode = "branch")$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2
) / 2

homemade_f3
```

We can see that when we specify `mode = "branch"`, the returned values of $f$
statistics correspond to the _real branch lengths_ in terms of times! Which is
quite cool because as we discussed, the mathematical expectation of $f_3$
statistic does, in fact, represent the overlap of paths in a tree going from p1
and p2 to the outgroup p4:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model)
```

:::


Hopefully, you can now appreciate that there's nothing magical about $f$
statistics. Even though their practical interpretation can get sometimes
complicated, internally they _always_ boil down to tracing paths through
population trees in order to obtain statistical expectations of allele frequency
correlations between lineages under study, easily visualized by tracing paths
through population trees.

In a way, setting `mode = "branch"` can be understood as instructing _slendr_ to
compute the results --- in this case, of the $f_3$ statistic --- in "real time
units", generations.











## Exercise: Basic intuition into the $f_4$ statistic

Now let's finally dig into exploring the most critical component of population
genetics research (particularly in the context of ancient DNA)---the venerable
$f_4$-statistic, formally established by Nick Patterson and David Reich in
2008.

From the [intuitive follow-up paper on $f$-statistics by Benjamin
Peter](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214), we know
that (in a very similar way to $f_2$ and $f_3$) $f_4(W, X; Y, Z)$ statistic can
be interpreted as the overlap between the paths in a tree connecting the pairs
W-X and Y-Z, as is demonstrated in [Figure
1](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/figure/379128872/1485fig1.jpeg) of the
linked paper.

That said, what value does any given $f_4$ statistic _actually_ gives you of
course depends on the (in practice, hidden) underlying demographic model which
determines how populations are related---in fact, what we usually need to do is
to infer features of that hidden model---and also what do we assign into each
of the four positions of the $f_4$ "quartet configuration".

---

**Knowing the relationships between populations encoded by the tree model
programmed in your script `f_null.R` and the interpretation of the $f_4$
statistic, what is the expected value of $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$ for this model?
Try to answer by taking a look at the sketch of your model and tracing the path
overlaps between p1-p2 and p3-p4, then compute the statistic on a `ts`
simulated data with the `ts_f4()` function to verify your intuition. Does your
simulation give you the _exact_ result you might expect based on the
visualization of the model alone? If it doesn't give you the exact expected
result, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### click to see the solution

As we can see below, $f$-statistics theory tells us that the value should be
zero, but without having a reference baseline, we get a number which is very
tiny (the value in the `f4` column). But how tiny would it have to be to be
"basically zero"?

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

The reason we didn't get _exactly_ zero is stochastic noise of any evolutionary
process, which means that that along a genome (even a small one, only 10 Mb of
simulated sequence) there are many possible trees. Sometimes, [incomplete
lineage sorting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_lineage_sorting) will
lead to genealogical trees which do not fit the expected "well-behaved"
population tree like the one we see when we run `plot_model()`.

That said, gene trees that don't fit the overall population trees will tend to
"average out", particularly when we look across many different regions of the
genome---this is why the simulated $f_4$ gets very close to zero.

:::

---

As suggested in the solution above, the reason we don't get a perfectly zero
expected value of the $f_4$ is because of ILS and stochasticity. Let's test
this hypothesis now.

**First, evaluate `ts` in your R console and note how many trees do you have in
your 10 Mb tree-sequence.**

**Now, restart your R session (`Session -> Restart R`). Then, temporarily
change the `N`** (which, in this case, really is $N_e$)** of all populations in
your model to 1 and re-run your script to get a new `ts` and compute the same
$f_4$ statistic again. $N_e$ of one implies a ludicrously high amount of drift,
which should eliminate ILS completely, giving us $f_4$ close to its
mathematical expectation of zero. Is this true? How many trees does your tree
sequence have now?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
ts_num_trees <- ts$num_trees
```

We changed all N sizes to 1, then we rerun the entire script `f_statistics.R`
again:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

# !!!
# note the temporary change to N = 1
# !!!
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Now let's compute the $f_4$ again on the `ts` tree sequence produced by this
extreme model:

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

Indeed, when we type `ts` into the R console, we see that it only contains
`{r} ts$num_trees`
individual trees compared to the previous count of
`{r} ts_num_trees`,
consistent with an absolutely extreme amounts of genetic drift in your model.

:::

---

Of course, changing $N_e$ to value of 1 as we did above is a drastic measure of
only theoretical utility. We could hardly get away with doing that, if we wanted
to use simulations to make a point in our research paper.

How do we deal with the unavoidable stochasticity in our simulations then? This
wasn't much of a problem in exercises in the previous chapters, but we need the
way to solve this to be able to get useful, applicable results.

Let's look into this now.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

:::






## Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates

As a means to tame the stochasticity and help meaningful statistical patterns
stand out, I recently implemented a new _slendr_ function `ts_replicates()`,
specifically for this workshop! The way it works is like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts_replicate(
  n = <number of replicates to simulate>,
  {
    # ...
    # a block of slendr code wrapped in { ... } containing a ts simulation
    # and a statistical computation we want to run in given replicates
    # ...
  }
)
```

---

**Take a look at its manual page under `?ts_replicates`, then use it to run 10
replicate simulations of the $f_4$ statistic above** (the one which should give
us a zero expectation, but it wasn't clear if it did or not), **saving the
result to variable `df`. What format does the result have? When you visualize
the distribution of $f_4$ values across all 10 replicates, are they more
interpretable in terms of the statistical expectation for this particular $f_4$
quartet?**

::: aside

**Note:** If you want to speed up the replicate simulation, note that
`?ts_replicate` allows running multiple simulations in parallel.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how we can modify the "template" above to answer this question:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(

  # run 10 replicates ...
  n = 10,

  # ... of the following block of code...
  {

  # ... which first simulates a tree sequence ...
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # ... and then computes a data frame with the given f4 statistic ...
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])

  } # ... the function automatically binds all data frames into single one
)

```

We can see that we get the same format of the data frame as normally produced by
the `ts_f4()` function, except with a new column `rep` added, indicating a
replicate number.

```{r}
df
```

This means we can visualize their distribution easily like this, for example:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

As we can see, when we run multiple replicates of the simulation, we are able to
"control" the stochastic noise a bit, making the expected pattern stand out more
clearly: we see that the expected value of `{r} unique(df$statistic)` is really
zero (up to that unavoidable stochastic noise shown by the scatter of individual
replicate values around zero).

:::







## Exercise: Other $f_4$ "quartets"

Of course, $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$ is only one possible "quartet configuration".

**Expand your 10 replicates simulation $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$ by adding the
computation of $f_4(p1, p3; p2, p4)$ and $f_4(p1, p4; p2, p3)$ in the same `{
... }` block provided to `ts_replicate()` (making sure you `rbind()` all three
data resulting frames together at the end).**

**How would you compare the interpretation of the three $f_4$ statistics,
looking at your sketch of the four-population model (or by looking at the
visualization of the model below), before running and visualizing the expanded
replication code you just wrote? Again, use sketching of paths on a population
tree on paper to try to figure it out first based on the definition of what
$f_4$ between two pairs of lineages indicate. Does your interpretation fit what
you get from the simulation once you run it?**


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's add the computation of all three $f_4$ statistics in the same replicate
simulation pipeline:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  # instead of computing one f4 like before, we compute all three and then
  # bind the three data frames into a single one
  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"]), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"]), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

We get a data frame with multiple replicates for each of the three statistics:

```{r}
df
```

From the mathematical definition of $f_4$ as internal branch lengths between two
pairs of lineages in a given "quartet" and knowing the topological structure of
our population tree, we can predict that the first $f_4$ is expected to be zero
(which is what we established earlier), and the other two $f_4$ statistics are
expected to have the same value representing the internal branch length
connecting pairs p1-p2 and p3-p4.

This is exactly what we see in our results:

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

:::

---

**Make a copy of your `ts_replicate()` code computing the three $f_4$ statistics
and modify it by setting `mode = "branch"`, as we did before, perhaps changing
`df` to `df_branch` for easier reference. Recall that `mode = "branch"`
instructs _slendr_'s internal statistical machinery to use "model time units"
(here, generations) in computing the results based on branches, instead of
mutations. When you visualize the three $f_4$ statistics computed in this way,
do you see this being reflected in the scale (and meaning) of the numbers which
you get back?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's save the result in a new data frame `df_branch`:

```{r}
df_branch <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

When we visualize the results, we do indeed see that the `f4` column contains
the expected branch lengths expressed in real generation times! Here are the
results plotted alongside the model using the package _cowplot_ (from which the
branch length times can be read more easily):

```{r}
library(cowplot) # get access to the plot_grid() function

plot_grid(
  # first panel:
  plot_model(model, schedule = schedule),

  # second panel:
  ggplot(df_branch, aes(statistic, f4)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_jitter() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed"),

  # plot both panels in two rows:
  nrow = 2
)
```

:::










## Catch up

This was a lot of work! If you want to check in with the state of our
$f$-statistics exploratory simulation script `f_null.R`, here it is in the form
which showcases the most important results from this chapter so far:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the entire script

```{r}
#| echo: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

:::











## Exercise: Interpreting $f_4$ as an admixture hypothesis test

Admittedly, thinking about $f$ statistics as measures of allele frequency
correlations between populations and interpreting them as overlapping branch
lengths is intellectually interesting in terms of population genetics theory),
but in practice, they are most famous (and most famously used) as admixture
tests.

**Create a new script `f_admixture.R` and copy my solutions to the exercises in
this chapter available under the _"Catch up"_ section above into that script.**
This is just to get the same starting point. **Restart your R session (`Session
-> Restart R`) then skim through this script and re-run it. Having gone through
the exercises, the code should look somewhat familiar and the visualization you
obtain by typing out `p_panels` into your R console (the branch lengths encoded
by the three $f_4$ statistics we studied) should make sense.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the final visualization of the three $f_3$ statistics for easier
reference as you work on the following exercise.

```{r}
#| echo: false
p_panels
```

:::


---

Right now our script `f_admixture.R` doesn't have any admixture! It still
contains what we established in this chapter so far: a statistical null model of
"nothing interesting happened in the demographic history in terms of potential
admixture", as is reflected in the $f_4$ values we obtained.

**Introduce the following two changes to the `f_admixture.R` script to turn it
into an admixture model:**

1. **Program a `gene_flow()` event `gf`, introducing 20% gene-flow from p3 to px
between 400 and 300 generations ago.**

2. **Add this `gf` event into the `model` compilation step executed by
`compile_model().**

**With the steps 1. and 2. done, your model now includes admixture. Re-run the
script again, and inspect the final visualization obtained by typing out
`p_panels` into your R console. You should see an admixture edge added to your
population tree.**

**How does admixture from p3 to px affect the branch lengths compared to the
previous model `f_null.R` of no admixture? Pay particular attention to the
$f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ statistic which had an expected value of zero before---does
it still have a zero value? If not, why, and what does it tell us about it
utility to study admixture histories?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's only the final visualization of the figure in the `p_panel` variable:

```{r}
#| echo: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p3, to = px, start = 400, end = 300, proportion = 0.2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

As we can see, because of the admixture event, our previously tree-like
population model is no longer tree. In the tree model without an admixture edge,
there was no path overlap between the pairs p1-p2 and p3-p4, which is why the
$f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ statistic was zero.

Admixture is a violation of "treeness", because "mathematical" trees are not
allowed to have edges (they effectively create "loops" in the
trees)---structures which do have edges are called "admixture graphs", This is
why the statistic now significantly deviates from zero.

This is exactly why $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ is useful as a statistical hypothesis
test of admixture---if a population quartet is from a truly tree-like model,
this statistic will always necessarily be zero; conversely, it can only ever be
non-zero if the underlying model (usually hidden, in real-world applications)
involves admixture which violates "treeness".

:::

This is exactly why $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ is useful as a statistical hypothesis
test of admixture---if a population quartet is from a truly tree-like model,
this statistic will always necessarily be zero; conversely, it can only ever be
non-zero if the underlying model (usually hidden, in real-world applications)
involves admixture which violates "treeness".






## Exercise: Estimating admixture proportions

From the little simulation and tree-doodling experiments above we now got a
sense of how various $f$ statistics (and particularly $f_4$ statistics)
mathematically quantify allele frequency correlations between lineages of
population trees and how they can be interpreted as the amounts of overlaps of
paths traced along branches of those trees. We also got an idea how different
patterns emerge in $f_4$ statistic expectation when gene-flow is introduced into
population trees, adding admixture edges to them and turning them into so-called
"admixture graphs".

It turns out that the same principles allow us to not just test the hypothesis
of whether an admixture event happened in the history of our samples, but also
estimate the proportion of ancestry derived from admixture.

```{r}
f4ratios <- ts_replicate(
  n = 20,
  {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
    
  # one possible "f4-ratio" variant
  num1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  den1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  
  # another possible "f4-ratio" variant
  num2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  den2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  
  # create a data frame with both variants
  data.frame(estimate = c("variant1", "variant2"),
             prop = c(num1 / den1, prop2 = num2 / den2))
  },
  parallel = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_f4ratios <-  ggplot(f4ratios, aes(prop, color = estimate)) +
    geom_density() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.2, 0.8), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1))

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_f4ratios, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```







## Exercise: Masking evidence of admixture?

In another amazing [follow-up
paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11563031/) on $f$ statistics and
admixture graphs which provides advice and guidance on performing admixture analyses,
the author writes the following:

> two admixture events together can cause an $f_4$-statistic to be close to zero
and thereby mask the signal of admixture

Obviously, this can be a rather worrisome, because real-world population histories
are very complex and involve, of course, multiple admixture events across our idealized population trees.

**Try to modify your admixture model by introducing such second gene-flow event,
which would make the $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ statistic (which we established serves
as an admixture test) return back to a near-zero expectation, and therefore mask
evidence of p3-p2 admixture even though we know it happened in the simulation.**
